title: Nobody Fixes Anything Any More
subtitle: A school repair club that started with one broken kettle
text: The repair club at Northbridge School meets on Thursdays, in a technology room that smells faintly of solder. It was started eighteen months ago by two fifteen-year-olds who had no particular skills and no equipment at all. {0} By the end of that first term they had mended sixty-three things.

The club began, as these things often do, by accident. Priya Raval's kettle had stopped working and her father was about to throw it out. {1} It took her four evenings and a video she barely understood, but the kettle still boils today.

Word spread more quickly than either of them expected. Teachers began leaving items on the desk by the door, usually without explanation. {2} Most weeks there is also at least one thing nobody can identify.
Not everything can be saved, and learning to say so was the hardest lesson. {3} A modern laptop, by contrast, is often designed in a way that makes opening it almost impossible without breaking it.
The club keeps a record of every repair, and the numbers tell an odd story. {4} The failure is almost always a single cheap component that costs less than a bus fare.

What surprises visitors most is the noise. People imagine a room of quiet concentration, and it is nothing of the sort. {5} The arguments are usually about method and almost never about who gets the credit.
Priya has now left the school, and the club has thirty-one members. {6}
sentences: Toasters, lamps and headphones arrive constantly; bicycles arrive in spring; printers arrive in a state of open hostility.
Instead she asked whether she could take it apart first, on the kitchen table, with a screwdriver borrowed from a neighbour.
Roughly two-thirds of the objects brought in are not broken in any serious sense at all.
Nobody there can explain why so many of them are older brothers and sisters of the original members.
Repairs are done in pairs, and pairs argue.
All they had was permission to use the room and a note on the noticeboard inviting people to bring in anything that no longer worked.
An old radio can usually be rescued, because it was built at a time when somebody expected it to be repaired.
The club charges nothing, and has never accepted a donation from anyone.
